books.title: Northanger Abbey
books.author: Jane Austen
books.desc: Seventeen-year-old Catherine Morland, raised on gothic novels, discovers Bath society and an old abbey in Jane Austen's sparkling, funny coming-of-age novel.
about: Catherine Morland, the cheerful daughter of a country clergyman, is invited to spend a season in Bath. There she meets the lively Isabella Thorpe and her boastful brother John, and the witty Henry Tilney and his sister Eleanor. When the Tilneys invite her to their family home, Northanger Abbey, Catherine's imagination, fed by gothic novels, begins to see secrets in every room.

The novel is both a love story and a gentle parody of the gothic fiction that was popular at the time, especially Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho. Austen laughs at the conventions of these books while defending the pleasure of reading novels, and she follows how a young woman learns to tell the difference between fiction and the real people around her.

Northanger Abbey was the first novel Austen completed for publication, but it appeared only after her death, in December 1817, together with Persuasion. It remains one of her most playful books and has been adapted several times for film and television.

books.title: My Ántonia
books.author: Willa Cather
books.desc: An orphaned boy on the Nebraska prairie and a Bohemian immigrant girl grow up together in Willa Cather's moving portrait of pioneer life.
about: Jim Burden, now a lawyer in New York, remembers his childhood in Nebraska. Orphaned at ten, he travels west to live with his grandparents and arrives on the same train as the Shimerdas, a poor family of Bohemian immigrants. Their eldest daughter, Ántonia, becomes his friend, and the novel follows both of them from the hard early years on the prairie to their lives as young adults.

Told as a memoir, the book is a portrait of a place and of a person. Cather writes with great simplicity about the land, the seasons and the immigrant families who struggled to farm it, and about the strength of a woman who stays true to herself.

My Ántonia was published in 1918 and is often grouped with O Pioneers! and The Song of the Lark as Cather's 'Prairie Trilogy'. It is widely considered one of the great American novels of the early twentieth century.

books.title: Looking Backward
books.author: Edward Bellamy
books.desc: A Bostonian falls asleep in 1887 and wakes up in the year 2000, in a peaceful society without poverty. One of the most influential utopian novels ever written.
about: Julian West, a wealthy young man from Boston, suffers from insomnia and sleeps in an underground room. In 1887 he is put into a deep trance and wakes up in the year 2000. He is taken in by Dr. Leete and his family, who show him a city transformed: no poverty, no strikes, no money in the old sense, and a society organised as one great cooperative.

The story is a framework for long conversations in which Dr. Leete explains how the new society works, from industry and shops to education and the role of women. Bellamy uses Julian's surprise to criticise the inequality and waste of his own century.

Looking Backward was one of the best-selling American books of the nineteenth century. It inspired Nationalist clubs across the United States and many replies and imitations, and it remains a key text in the history of utopian fiction.

books.title: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
books.author: Edgar Allan Poe
books.desc: A stowaway, a mutiny, shipwreck and a voyage toward the South Pole: Edgar Allan Poe's only complete novel is a dark and strange sea adventure.
about: Arthur Gordon Pym, a young man from Nantucket, hides aboard the whaling ship Grampus with the help of his friend Augustus. His adventure quickly turns into a nightmare of mutiny, storm, shipwreck and starvation. Later, rescued by another ship, he sails far into the unknown seas of the South Pole, where stranger and stranger things begin to happen.

Poe mixes the style of real travel accounts, with dates, positions and technical details, with horror and mystery. The book moves from a realistic sea story to something closer to a dream, and its open, enigmatic ending has puzzled readers for generations.

Published in 1838, it is Poe's only complete novel. It influenced later writers, notably Jules Verne, who wrote a sequel, An Antarctic Mystery (1897), and H. P. Lovecraft. The book also contains dated and offensive depictions of non-white characters, typical of its time.

books.title: The Velveteen Rabbit
books.author: Margery Williams Bianco
books.desc: A stuffed rabbit given to a little boy on Christmas morning longs to become Real. A short, tender classic about love and growing up.
about: On Christmas morning a little boy finds a velveteen rabbit in his stocking. At first the rabbit is forgotten among the more expensive mechanical toys, but the wise old Skin Horse tells him that a toy becomes Real when a child truly loves it for a long time. Slowly the rabbit becomes the boy's favourite companion, through games, bedtimes and a serious illness.
The story is short and simple, but it speaks about love, loss and what it means to be real. Its gentle tone makes it a favourite for reading aloud, for children and adults alike.
The Velveteen Rabbit, or How Toys Become Real was first published in 1922 with illustrations by William Nicholson. It was Margery Williams's best-known book and has never been out of print.
books.author_short: English-American children's author (1881–1944), best known for The Velveteen Rabbit.
author_long: Margery Williams was born in London in 1881 and moved to the United States as a child. She married the Italian bookseller Francesco Bianco and lived in England, Italy and finally New York, where she died in 1944.

She wrote novels for adults before turning to children's books. The Velveteen Rabbit (1922) made her famous, and she went on to write many other stories, including Poor Cecco (1925) and Winterbound (1936), which received a Newbery Honor.
